title: Minimum Number of Valid Strings to Form Target II
statement:
You get a list of strings `words` and a string `target`. Call a string **valid** when it is non-empty and at least one string in `words` starts with it, meaning it equals the first few letters (possibly all) of that word.

Cut `target` into consecutive valid pieces that, read left to right, spell `target` exactly, and return the smallest number of pieces such a cut can use. Pieces may repeat, and one word may supply any number of them. If `target` cannot be cut this way at all, return `-1`.
constraints: The total length of all words is at most 10^5
words[i] contains only lowercase English letters
target contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Every prefix of a word is itself a prefix of that word, so if some word matches `target` for `L` letters starting at position `i`, then pieces of every length from 1 to `L` may start at `i`. Let `reach[i]` be the longest such match over all words. The task then becomes Jump Game II: from position `i` you may jump to any position up to `i + reach[i]`; find the fewest jumps from 0 to `n`. Trying every piece from every start (the brute force, and the DP of version I) costs O(n · L) when words are long, so we need `reach` fast. The **Z-function** gives, for one word, its match length at every target position in linear time.

## Approach

1. For each `word`, build `text = word + '#' + target`. The `#` appears nowhere else, so no match can run past the word.
2. Compute the Z-array: `z[i]` is the length of the longest common prefix of `text` and `text[i..]`. The box `[left, right)` is the match reaching furthest right so far; inside it, `z[i]` starts from the copy `z[i - left]` (capped at `right - i`) instead of 0, which makes the pass linear.
3. Position `i` of `target` sits at `word.length + 1 + i` in `text`; keep the best value over all words in `reach[i]`.
4. Greedy jumps: scan `i` while tracking `farthest = max(i + reach[i])`. When `i` reaches `end`, the edge of what `pieces` pieces cover, add a piece: if `farthest` did not pass `end`, return `-1`; otherwise `pieces++` and `end = farthest`.
5. Return `pieces`.

## Example 1, step by step

`words = ["abc", "aaaaa", "bcdef"]`, `target = "aabcdabc"`. The matches give `reach = [2, 3, 3, 0, 0, 3, 2, 0]` (for example `reach[2] = 3` because "bcdef" matches "bcd").

- `i = 0`: `farthest = 2`; `i === end`, so `pieces = 1`, `end = 2`.
- `i = 1`: `farthest = 4`. `i = 2`: `farthest = 5`, `i === end`, so `pieces = 2`, `end = 5`.
- `i = 3, 4` add nothing; `i = 5`: `farthest = 8`, `i === end`, so `pieces = 3`, `end = 8`.

The answer is 3: "aa" + "bcd" + "abc".

## Complexity

- Time: O(S + k · n) for k words of total length S and `n = target.length`: each Z pass is linear in `word.length + n`, and the jumps take O(n). (Rolling hashes with binary search, or Aho-Corasick, remove the factor k.)
- Space: O(max word length + n) for one `text` and its `z`, plus `reach`.

## Pitfalls

- Always taking the longest piece fails: with `["ab", "bcdefg"]` and `"abcdefg"`, "ab" strands you at "c", while "a" + "bcdefg" uses 2.
- The separator must be a character that no word or target contains.
- Return `-1` as soon as `farthest` stops passing `end`; otherwise the loop counts pieces that do not exist.
- A word longer than the rest of `target` is fine: `z` stops at the end of `text`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `target` |
| `reach` | `reach[i]` is the longest valid piece starting at `i` |
| `word`, `text` | the word being matched, and `word + '#' + target` |
| `z` | Z-array of `text` |
| `left`, `right` | the Z-box `[left, right)` that reaches furthest right |
| `pieces` | pieces used so far |
| `end` | how far `pieces` pieces can spell |
| `farthest` | how far one more piece can spell |
